U.S. Representative Chellie Pingree Skip to Content KNOW YOUR RIGHTS : Interacting with ICE & Immigration Officers Meet Chellie Chellie Pingree never anticipated a life in politics. Living on the offshore island of North Haven, Maine, she raised her kids and ran a small business. She served on the school board and as the local tax assessor, a job no one else in town wanted. But in 1991, when she was approached about running for State Senate, she jumped at the chance. Curbing Fast Fashion Pollution | U.S. Representative Chellie Pingree Fast&nbsp;fashion&nbsp;has become&nbsp;<b>hugely popular</b>&nbsp;with consumers. But it comes at a&nbsp;<b>high cost</b>&nbsp;<b>to our planet.</b></p> <p>Today, nearly two-thirds of all the fibers we wear and use are made from oil. The&nbsp;fashion industry is now responsible for<strong> more carbon emissions than all international flights and maritime shipping combined</strong>.</p> <p>Fast&nbsp;fashion&nbsp;relies on cheap manufacturing, frequent consumption, and short-lived garment use. This constant cycle of production and disposal is taking a huge toll on our environment. So much so that satellite images have identified a pile of discarded clothing in Chile sent there from Europe, Asia, and America&nbsp;<b>so large, <a href="https://www.space.com/mountain-discarded-clothes-chile-satellite-photo">it can be seen from space</a></b>.&nbsp;</p> <div style="text-align: center;"> <table cellpadding="5" style="width: 896.333333px; height: 816.333333px;"> <tbody> <tr> <td style="text-align: center;"><img alt="" src="https://pingree.house.gov/UploadedPhotos/HighResolution/2eafffcf-5cfb-4e1e-a21c-217b96c57e35.jpg" width="1000" height="800" style="vertical-align: middle;" /></td> </tr> </tbody> </table> </div> <p>In 2018,&nbsp;<b>17 million tons of textiles were generated in the U.S.</b>&nbsp;As the rate that clothing is produced and discarded increases, only 15% of clothing in the U.S. is recycled or reused, with the rest either incinerated or sent to landfills for disposal.</p> <p>This same period has seen a significant increase in textile waste, as clothes, many never worn, make their way to landfills.&nbsp;Rebuilding and revitalizing U.S. sustainable fiber production and processing, known as “reshoring,” are key to reversing these trends.&nbsp;</p> <p>In addition, over the past several decades, hundreds of thousands of fiber and textil
